title: Development of a Gene Therapy for UBA5 Deficiency
text:
UBA5 deficiency is an ultra-rare monogenic disease with neurological presentations which results in death of
most patients in the childhood as there is no treatment for it. Lack of a viable mammalian model of UBA5
deficiency has prevented therapeutic development. This proposal aims to characterize the first viable mouse
model of UBA5 disease which has patient presentations, find biomarkers for the disease, and perform efficacy
studies of AAV gene therapy using the candidate that shown to be efficacious in the preliminary studies of this
mouse model.

title: Metabolic Reprogramming of Myeloid Cells to Enhance Cancer Immunotherapy
text: A major mechanism of immunotherapeutic resistance is immune suppression and major cell types that drive immune suppression are myeloid-derived suppressor cells and M2-like tumor associated macrophages, which compromise anti-cancer immunity. We identified separate pharmacologic approaches rendering them less suppressive, thus, raising tumor susceptibility to novel immunotherapy regimens. Here, we are investigating strategies to optimize this therapeutic paradigm in solid cancer models and the underlying immune mechanisms, which will have important translational implications in cancer patients.

title: Physics and Biology in Medicine Research Training
text:
This training grant aims to continue to develop research scientists that are well versed in physics, biology,
mathematics, chemistry, engineering and computer science, and who also understand the application of these
disciplines to the instruments and techniques used in the diagnosis, monitoring and treatment of disease as well
as research fields that help us understand basic mechanisms of disease. These scientists will become actively
involved in research into new methods that seek earlier diagnosis of disease as well as more specific (patient
specific, disease specific) treatments of disease in many clinical applications.

title: Retrograde TGN/Golgi transport and nuclear targeting of HPV during entry
text:
High-risk human papillomaviruses (HPVs) are responsible for essentially all cancers of the uterine cervix, as
well as many other anogenital and oropharyngeal cancers. Despite the availability of highly effective
prophylactic vaccines against HPV infection, cancers due to HPV infection remain a major disease burden
worldwide due to the limited use of the vaccine and the absence of vaccine benefit in people with current HPV
infection. Because illuminating the molecular mechanisms of HPV infection may lead to valuable new
strategies to combat HPV infection and reveal new biological principles, in this application we will elucidate
critical steps during HPV entry into cells.

title: Inhibition of viral membrane fusion by interferon-induced proteins
text:
Interferon-induced transmembrane proteins (IFITMs) inhibit entry of diverse enveloped viruses upon expression
in target cells and upon incorporation into progeny virions. While rigidification of cell membranes (“tough
membrane” model) has been widely accepted as the universal mechanism for IFITMs' antiviral activity, our
results challenge this hypothesis and support a multi-faceted model instead. We will apply innovative imaging
and biophysical approaches to elucidate the mechanistic differences between the two modes of virus restriction
by IFITMs.

title: De Novo Synthesis of Collagen-Like Polymers for Biomedical Applications
text:
The project is focused on the development of a new collagen-like synthetic polymer as a potential replacement
of animal-derived collagen for biomedical applications such as tissue and organ engineering, drug delivery, and
wound healing. The synthetic collagen-like polymer would help to eliminate the safety and contamination
concerns of animal-derived collagen. In addition, the proposed synthetic route may open the door to synthesis
of other polymeric biomaterials based on short repeatable peptide sequences like ELP or RGD peptides.

title: Characterizing the behavioral and neural mechanisms of inhibitory control dysfunction in PTSD.
text:
Many hallmark PTSD symptoms including intrusive trauma-related thoughts and feelings, poor
concentration, and risk-taking, reflect deficits in inhibitory control. Inhibitory control impairments, and
dysfunction in the underlying neural circuits, are linked to poor long-term outcomes following traumatic
stress, contributing to the development and maintenance of PTSD, poorer functional outcomes, and reduced
treatment efficacy. The goal of the current proposal is to comprehensively characterize the nature and
specificity of inhibitory control deficits in PTSD, their neural basis, and how they impact PTSD in everyday
life. These studies will advance mechanistic models of PTSD and lead to better diagnostic tools and more
individualized treatments. Further, they will inform which existing inhibitory control treatments would be
most useful to complement existing front-line PTSD treatments and provide much-needed neurocognitive
targets to develop novel PTSD treatments.

title: Deciphering tumor-immune coevolution during metastatic progression
text:
In the United States, over 600,000 people die of cancer each year, and the majority of these deaths are a
consequence of metastasis, not primary tumor growth. Interactions between tumors and the immune system
during metastasis are distinct from those in the primary tumor, yet while immunotherapies represent the greatest
advances in the treatment of stage IV metastatic disease, little is known about immune responses during
metastasis. In this project, we are uncovering how tumors and the immune system coevolve during metastasis
to better understand how metastatic tumors escape immune responses and how to tip this balance in favor of
anti-tumor immunity.

title: Intercellular Transfer of Mitochondria at the Nerve-Cancer Interface
text:
Innervation of cancer tissue plays a crucial role in aggressive disease, yet how cancer cells and neurons
communicate during this process remains poorly understood. Our project investigates how infiltrating nerves
transfer their mitochondria to breast cancer cells, leading to increased metabolism of cancer cells, signaling
changes, and dissemination of cancer cells to distal sites. We aim to uncover the underlying mechanisms and
consequences of inhibiting these transfers to aid the future development of novel approaches that inhibit cancer
metastasis.

title: Mechanism of double-negative T cells in antitumor immunity to breast cancer
text:
Breast cancers are poorly immunogenic, which significantly hampers breast cancer
immunotherapy. The finding that DN T cells can inhibit tripe-negative breast cancer growth is
novel and has not been explored. Deciphering the cellular and molecular mechanism of how DN
T cells orchestrate antitumor immune response in breast cancer will fundamentally advance our
knowledge in tumor immunology and allow us to develop more effective DN T cell-based cancer
immunotherapy for breast cancer treatment.

title: Human-mouse platform for data-driven patient stratification, target discovery, and validation in GBM
text:
This proposal seeks to better understand the tumor microenvironment mechanisms that shape two newly
defined glioblastoma (GBM) mesenchymal subtypes, which differ in patients' survival, genetic drivers, and
myeloid cell compositions. Our data-driven approach uses machine learning, single-cell, and spatial
transcriptomic data across a large human GBM cohort to dissect the tumor microenvironment and identify
therapeutically relevant immunomodulators associated with these distinct GBM mesenchymal subtypes. In
parallel, we will develop and comprehensively immunophenotype genetically engineered mouse models of the
newly defined mesenchymal subtypes, which will provide a pre-clinical validation platform for the therapeutic
targets identified in this proposal and in future studies.

title: Pfn1’s Role in Genomic Stability and Immune Response in Breast Cancer
text:
Immune checkpoint blockade immunotherapy is a promising treatment for breast cancer patients, most critically
for triple-negative breast cancer patients who have the worst overall prognosis given the lack of targeted
therapies. The goal of this project is to determine whether and how genetic disruption of the gene encoding
Profilin-1, an actin-binding protein, promotes the existence of an anti-tumor immune environment, thus increasing
the efficacy of immunotherapy. If successful, the completion of these studies will elucidate a novel mechanistic
link between Pfn1 loss and an anti-tumor immune response and lay the conceptual foundation for the inhibition
of Pfn1 as a therapeutic supplement to immunotherapy.

title: Lifespan Regulation by Inter-Organellar Heme Signaling
text:
This project addresses how heme, an essential iron containing nutrient, cofactor, and signaling molecule,
serves as an inter-organellar and inter-organ signal that regulates lifespan in cells and animals.
Understanding the molecular processes that govern organismal and cellular aging will be critical for new
therapies that can help extend lifespan and healthspan and mitigate aging related diseases.

title: Noninvasive Cardiovascular Imaging Research Training Program
text:
The proposed competing application of our T32 training program is designed to train
clinician-scientists in cardiovascular imaging to prepare them for successful and
productive academic careers. The program offers mutli-disciplinary training in a broad
and diverse spectrum of areas in cardiovascular medicine with relevance to imaging
science. With this renewal, we continue our primary goals of providing leadership in
academic cardiovascular imaging and training future leaders in imaging science to
improve outcomes in cardiovascular disease.

title: Core B: Biospecimen Core
text:
CORE B – BIOSPECIMEN CORE: PROJECT NARRATIVE
Biospecimen Core (Core B), provides a variety of clinically annotated samples (tumor, normal skin, plasma,
peripheral blood lymphocytes, tumor infiltrating lymphocytes, serum, short term cultures, DNA and RNA) to
SPORE investigators and other collaborators at Yale and outside of Yale. Integration with Core C for storage of
data is key to maximizing utilization of specimens and distribution of samples is governed by a Tissue Committee.
The Core is central to all the activities of YSPORE and well integrated with pathology and clinical services at
Yale Cancer Center.

title: TEAMSPORT to Community TEAMSPORT: Validating and Adapting a Precision Oncology Reflex Testing Team Intervention to Reduce Geographic Variation in Cancer Care Delivery
text:
PUBLIC HEALTH SIGNIFICANCE
Each year >500,000 Americans diagnosed with cancer have tumors that could be targeted with an FDA-
approved drug to treat their disease more effectively. However, there is wide variation in use of these treatments
in clinical practice. Rural patients, who are more likely to die from cancer than their non-rural counterparts, are
less likely to receive targeted cancer therapies and could benefit greatly from interventions to address this quality
gap.

title: Development and Support of the Pathway Tools Software
text:
The proposed project will generate software tools that increase the ability of scientists to leverage genome se-
quence data to advance human health. This software supports the creation of central database repositories and
websites containing genome data and data on cellular networks for disease-causing bacteria such as Mycobac-
terium tuberculosis. This project enables the development of more accurate predictions of the metabolic pathways
of disease-causing bacteria, and yields more accurate identification of anti-microbial drug targets.

title: Big Data Training for Cancer Research
text:
Big data, along with the associated computational and statistical tools, are transforming cancer research and
cancer care in almost all aspects. Built on our previous big data training courses for general biomedical
researchers and current big data training courses tailored for cancer researchers, this renewal project aims to
help cancer researchers develop essential analytical skills to extract knowledge from big data and find better
ways to understand, diagnose, and treat cancer. In addition, we will establish a big data community among
cancer researchers to foster collaboration and knowledge sharing to advance cancer research endeavors.

title: A single prime editing strategy for correcting diverse mutations responsible for RBM20-associated dilated cardiomyopathy
text:
Familial dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is a genetic heart condition that leads to a weakened heart muscle and
often requires a heart transplant, especially in young people. This project aims to develop a precise one-size-
fits-all gene editing method that can correct the genetic errors underlying DCM to improve heart cell function. If
successful, this approach has the potential to offer a single, one-time treatment for genetically diverse cases of
DCM and potentially other genetic conditions.

title: Investigating the Structural Basis of Human Glycine Receptor Modulation for Neurodevelopmental Disorders
text:
The glycine receptor type alpha 2 (GlyRα2) plays a role in neurogenesis, and mutations have been linked to
neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism spectrum disorder and epilepsy. By investigating the
structure-function relationship and lipidic profile of GlyRα2, this study aims to provide a better understanding of
the role of this receptor in neurogenesis, adult physiology, and pathology. The knowledge gained from this
study may lead to the development of pharmacologic therapies targeting GlyRα2 to help alleviate the
symptoms of these disorders.
